problems.title: Quadratic bowl and one steepest descent step
problems.setup: f(x) = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with H = [[5,−1],[−1,5]] and b = (−9, −3). Start steepest descent at x₀ = (0, 0) with an exact line search.

parts.ask: Find the minimum value f* at the critical point x*.
Give the eigenvalues of H and the shape of the contours of f.
parts.a: λ = 4 along (1,1), λ = 6 along (1,−1); ellipses, long axis along (1,1)
w: λ = 4 along (1,−1), λ = 6 along (1,1); ellipses, long axis along (1,1)
λ = 4 along (1,1), λ = −6 along (1,−1); hyperbolas
λ = 5 twice; circles centred on x*
sol: Both eigenvalues positive: H is positive definite, contours are ellipses
Semi-axis length scales as 1/√λ, so the long axis lies along the λ = 4 direction

parts.ask: Find the exact line search step length α₀ along p₀ = −∇f(x₀).
Using α₀ = 5/22, find f(x₁).
sol: f(x₁) = −10.227, within 0.27 of f* after one step

problems.x: For a positive definite quadratic, x* = −H⁻¹b, the eigenvectors of H set the ellipse axes, and the exact steepest descent step is α = gᵀg / gᵀHg.

problems.title: A quadratic with a symmetric H
problems.setup: f(x) = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with H = [[2,6],[6,2]] and b = (−8, −8).

parts.ask: Find the value of f at the critical point.
Classify the critical point.
w: Minimum: eigenvalues 8 along (1,1) and 4 along (1,−1)
Maximum: eigenvalues −8 along (1,1) and −4 along (1,−1)
Saddle: eigenvalues 4 along (1,1) and −8 along (1,−1)
sol: Mixed eigenvalue signs give a saddle with hyperbolic contours

parts.ask: Evaluate f at x* + 2v with v = (1,−1)/√2.
Explain what a pure Newton step does from a point near this saddle, and what a descent method needs here.
parts.a: Newton jumps to the stationary point of the quadratic model, which is the saddle, since it solves Hp = −g regardless of curvature sign. A descent method needs a positive definite model (modified Hessian or trust region) to follow the negative curvature direction (1,−1) downhill.
sol: Newton step on a quadratic lands exactly on x* = (1,1)
Negative curvature direction (1,−1) gives unbounded decrease
Trust region or Hessian modification exploits that direction

problems.x: The eigenvalue signs of H classify a critical point, and f changes by ½λα² along each unit eigenvector.

problems.title: Wolfe check on an elliptic bowl
problems.setup: f(x) = x₁² + 4x₂², x₀ = (2, 1), search direction p = −∇f(x₀). Use Wolfe constants c₁ = 0.1 and c₂ = 0.5, and test the trial step α = 0.25.

parts.ask: Compute the directional derivative ∇f(x₀)ᵀp.
Does α = 0.25 satisfy the sufficient decrease (Armijo) condition?
w: No: f(x₀ + αp) = 5 > 4
Yes: f(x₀ + αp) = 3 ≤ 6
No: f(x₀ + αp) = 7 > 6

parts.ask: Check the curvature conditions at α = 0.25.
w: Both Wolfe conditions hold since 56 ≥ −40 and 56 ≥ 0
Weak Wolfe fails since the slope 56 is positive
Strong Wolfe holds since |56| ≤ |−80| = 80 here
sol: Strong: |56| ≤ c₂·80 = 40 fails: the step overshot the 1D minimum

parts.ask: Find the exact minimizing step along p.
sol: φ'(α) = ∇fᵀp + α pᵀHp = 0 with H = diag(2, 8)

problems.x: Strong Wolfe bounds |∇f(x + αp)ᵀp| by c₂|∇fᵀp|, which rejects steps that overshoot to a steep positive slope.

problems.title: Backtracking on a quartic
problems.setup: f(x) = x⁴ at x₀ = 1 with p = −f'(x₀) = −4, so φ(α) = (1 − 4α)⁴. Backtracking starts at α = 1, halves α each rejection, and uses c₁ = 0.1.

parts.ask: Compute φ'(0).
Find the accepted step length.
How many function evaluations did the line search use?
What does the Armijo test alone guarantee about the accepted step?
w: The exact 1D minimizer of φ
A curvature condition on φ'(α)
Global convergence with any initial α
sol: Armijo gives f(x₀ + αp) ≤ f(x₀) + c₁α∇fᵀp
Backtracking from a large α supplies steps long enough in practice

problems.x: Backtracking accepts the first trial step meeting φ(α) ≤ φ(0) + c₁αφ'(0), and the halving from α = 1 keeps steps long.

problems.title: Conjugate gradient on a 2x2 system
problems.setup: Minimize f(x) = ½xᵀAx − bᵀx with A = [[4,1],[1,3]] and b = (1, 2), using linear CG (Fletcher Reeves β) from x₀ = (0, 0).

parts.ask: Find the first step length α₀.
Find β₁.
After the second step, report x₂ component 2 (CG finishes in n = 2 steps).
Why does CG reach the exact solution in two iterations here?
parts.a: The directions are A-conjugate and n = 2
w: A is diagonal, so the two axes decouple
Fletcher Reeves β equals one at step two
The residuals are parallel to b
sol: Exact minimization over n A-conjugate directions gives x* in at most n steps

problems.x: Linear CG minimizes over successive A-conjugate directions and reaches x* in at most n steps in exact arithmetic.

problems.title: Newton step and a BFGS update
problems.setup: f(x) = x₁⁴ + x₂², x₀ = (1, 1). Take one pure Newton step, then form the BFGS update starting from B₀ = I using that step as s.

parts.ask: Find f(x₁) after the Newton step.
Compute yᵀs with s = x₁ − x₀ and y = ∇f(x₁) − ∇f(x₀).
What does the BFGS update B₁ satisfy, and why does yᵀs > 0 matter?
parts.a: B₁s = y; yᵀs > 0 keeps B₁ positive definite
w: B₁y = s; yᵀs > 0 makes the matrix B₁ diagonal
B₁s = y; yᵀs > 0 makes B₁ equal the true ∇²f(x₁)
B₁ = B₀; yᵀs > 0 sets the next line search step
sol: BFGS preserves positive definiteness when the curvature condition yᵀs > 0 holds

parts.ask: Compare the cost and convergence of Newton and BFGS for a large n problem.
parts.a: Newton needs the Hessian and an O(n³) solve each iteration but converges quadratically near x*. BFGS uses only gradients, updates in O(n²), and converges superlinearly.
sol: BFGS: rank two update from s and y, superlinear rate

problems.x: BFGS builds curvature from gradient differences through the secant condition B₁s = y, and yᵀs > 0 keeps the model positive definite.

problems.title: Dogleg step and radius update
problems.setup: f(x) = x₁⁴ + 2x₂² at x₀ = (1, 1) with model Hessian B = ∇²f(x₀) = diag(12, 4) and trust radius Δ = 1. Use the dogleg method, with η thresholds 0.25 and 0.75.

parts.ask: Find the length of the Cauchy (unconstrained steepest descent) point p_U.
Find the length of the full Newton step p_B.
sol: ‖p_B‖ = √(1/9 + 1) = 1.054 > Δ, so the dogleg path hits the boundary

parts.ask: The dogleg step is p = (−0.3551, −0.9348) on ‖p‖ = 1. Compute ρ = actual / predicted reduction.
What happens to the step and radius?
parts.a: Accept the step and expand Δ to 2
w: Reject the step and halve Δ to 0.5
Accept the step and halve Δ to 0.5
Accept the step and keep Δ = 1
sol: ρ = 1.06 > 0.75 and ‖p‖ = Δ: model is good and the boundary was active
Standard rule: Δ ← 2Δ = 2, x₁ = x₀ + p

problems.x: The dogleg path runs from the Cauchy point toward the Newton point and stops on the boundary, and ρ > 0.75 with an active boundary doubles Δ.

problems.title: Cauchy point with an indefinite model
problems.setup: A trust region model m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp has g = (3, 4), B = diag(2, −1) and Δ = 1.

parts.ask: Classify B.
w: Positive definite, eigenvalues 2 and 1
Negative definite, eigenvalues −2 and −1
Singular, eigenvalues 2 and 0
sol: Mixed signs give an indefinite model

parts.ask: Find τ in the Cauchy point p_C = −τΔ g/‖g‖.
Find the predicted reduction m(0) − m(p_C).
Explain why trust region methods handle this indefinite B safely.
parts.a: The constraint ‖p‖ ≤ Δ bounds the subproblem, so a minimizer exists for any symmetric B. The Cauchy point gives a guaranteed fraction of decrease, and negative curvature directions push the step to the boundary.
sol: Bounded region gives a well posed subproblem

problems.x: The Cauchy point minimizes the model along −g inside the region, with τ = 1 whenever gᵀBg ≤ 0 or the minimizer lies past Δ.

problems.title: KKT at a corner with two active constraints
problems.setup: Minimize f = (x₁ − 2)² + (x₂ − 2)² subject to g₁ = x₁ + 2x₂ − 3 ≤ 0 and g₂ = 2x₁ + x₂ − 3 ≤ 0. Use L = f + μ₁g₁ + μ₂g₂.

parts.ask: At the candidate x = (1, 1), which constraints are active?
w: Only g₁ = x₁ + 2x₂ − 3
Only g₂ = 2x₁ + x₂ − 3
Neither, (1,1) is interior

parts.ask: Solve stationarity for μ₁.
sol: μ₁ + 2μ₂ = 2 and 2μ₁ + μ₂ = 2 give μ₁ = μ₂ = 2/3

parts.ask: Is (1, 1) a KKT point?
w: No: μ₁ is negative, so stationarity fails at (1, 1)
No: two active constraints over-determine the point
Yes, but only with μ₁ = μ₂ = 0 and ∇f(1,1) = 0 too
sol: f is convex and the constraints are linear, so this KKT point is the global minimum f* = 2

parts.ask: Use μ₁ to estimate f* if g₁ is relaxed to x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 3.3.

problems.x: At a KKT corner, −∇f lies in the cone of active constraint gradients, and each μᵢ ≥ 0 is the sensitivity of f* to relaxing constraint i.

problems.title: Dropping a constraint with a negative multiplier
problems.setup: Minimize f = (x₁ − 1)² + (x₂ − 3)² subject to g₁ = x₁ + x₂ − 2 ≤ 0 and g₂ = x₁ − x₂ ≤ 0. Use L = f + μ₁g₁ + μ₂g₂.

parts.ask: At the corner (1, 1) with both constraints active, solve for μ₂.
sol: μ₁ + μ₂ = 0 and μ₁ − μ₂ = 4 give μ₁ = 2, μ₂ = −2

parts.ask: What does μ₂ = −2 tell you?
parts.a: Release g₂: moving off it lowers f
w: (1, 1) is the optimum
Release g₁: moving off it lowers f
The problem is infeasible
sol: μ₂ < 0 means f decreases into the interior of g₂, so g₂ is inactive at the optimum

parts.ask: With only g₁ active, find f*.
Find μ₁ at the optimum.

problems.x: An active set method releases any inequality whose multiplier is negative and re-solves with the remaining active constraints.

problems.title: Quadratic penalty versus log barrier
problems.setup: Minimize f = (x − 3)² subject to x ≤ 1, whose solution is x* = 1 with λ* = 4. Exterior penalty: f + (μ/2)max(0, x − 1)². Interior barrier: f − r ln(1 − x).

parts.ask: Find the penalty minimizer for μ = 10.
Estimate λ from the penalty solution at μ = 10.
sol: λ ≈ 3.33, approaching λ* = 4 as μ grows

parts.ask: Find the barrier minimizer for r = 0.1.
Compare the two sequences as μ → ∞ and r → 0.
parts.a: Penalty approaches x* from outside, barrier from inside
w: Penalty approaches x* from inside, barrier from outside
Both reach x* exactly at finite parameters
Both approach x* from the infeasible side
sol: Barrier multiplier estimate r/(1 − x) also tends to 4

problems.x: Exterior penalties converge from the infeasible side with λ ≈ μ·g, and log barriers converge from the feasible interior with λ ≈ r/(−g).

problems.title: One SQP step
problems.setup: Minimize f = x₁² + x₂² subject to h = x₁² + x₂ − 1 = 0 with L = f + λh. Start at x₀ = (1, 1) with λ₀ = 0, so the Lagrangian Hessian is W = 2I.

parts.ask: Which linear system gives the SQP step (p, λ₁)?
w: W p = −∇f with h ignored
sol: QP: min ∇fᵀp + ½pᵀWp s.t. h + Ap = 0

parts.ask: Solve for p₂, the x₂ component of the step.
Evaluate h at x₁ = x₀ + p.
sol: The residual equals p₁² = 0.04 from the curvature of h

parts.ask: Why does practical SQP use a merit function or filter?
parts.a: The full QP step can increase f or the constraint violation far from the solution. A merit function or filter judges each step on both objective and feasibility, which gives global convergence while keeping Newton speed near x*.
sol: Near x*, full steps give quadratic convergence of Newton on the KKT system

problems.x: SQP solves a QP with the Lagrangian Hessian and linearized constraints, which is Newton's method applied to the KKT conditions.

problems.title: Least squares line on four points
problems.setup: Fit ŷ = β₀ + β₁x to (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5) by least squares.

parts.ask: Find β₁ from the normal equations.
Compute the sum of squared residuals.
Compute R².
The surrogate predicts ŷ(4) = 6.5. What is the main caution?
parts.a: x = 4 is extrapolation beyond the sampled range
w: R² = 0.98 proves the line is exact at x = 4
The four residuals sum to a nonzero value
Four points give zero residual degrees of freedom
sol: Validate surrogates inside the sampled domain or with held out points

problems.x: Least squares solves XᵀXβ = Xᵀy, and with an intercept the residuals sum to zero and R² = 1 − SSE/SST.

problems.title: Gaussian RBF interpolation
problems.setup: Interpolate y(0) = 1 and y(1) = 2 with ŷ(x) = w₁φ(|x − 0|) + w₂φ(|x − 1|), φ(r) = exp(−r²).

parts.ask: Which matrix system gives w?
Solve for w₂.
Predict ŷ(0.5).
What does this surrogate predict far from the data, for example ŷ(3)?
w: It follows the linear data trend up to ŷ(3) = 4
It stays at the last sampled value, ŷ = 2
It grows without bound as x increases
sol: Gaussian basis functions vanish far from their centres
Adding a polynomial tail or using kriging with a trend captures behaviour far from samples

problems.x: RBF interpolation solves Φw = y so the surrogate passes through every sample, and Gaussian bases revert to zero away from the data.

problems.title: Finite difference versus complex step
problems.setup: Differentiate f(x) = eˣ at x = 0, where f'(0) = 1. Compare forward difference and central difference with h = 0.01, and complex step with h = 10⁻²⁰.

parts.ask: Find the forward difference error (estimate minus 1).
sol: Error ≈ h f''/2 = 0.005: first order in h

parts.ask: Find the central difference error.
sol: Error ≈ h² f'''/6 = 1.667×10⁻⁵: second order in h

parts.ask: Why can the complex step use h = 10⁻²⁰?
parts.a: It has no subtraction, so no cancellation
w: Imaginary parts are stored with extra mantissa bits
Its truncation error is exactly zero for every f
It averages the forward and backward differences
sol: Only truncation error O(h²) remains, so derivatives reach machine precision

parts.ask: Give the near optimal forward difference step for double precision (ε ≈ 2.2×10⁻¹⁶), as √ε.
sol: Balancing gives h ≈ √ε for f, f'' of order 1

problems.x: Finite differences trade truncation error against subtractive cancellation, while the complex step removes cancellation and gives derivatives to machine precision.

problems.title: Convexity check and gradient bound
problems.setup: f(x) = x₁² + x₁x₂ + x₂² + e^x₁.

parts.ask: Give the Hessian of f.
Find det ∇²f at the origin.
Why is f convex on all of ℝ²?
w: f is a sum of quadratic terms only, so it is convex
The Hessian is constant over the whole plane
det ∇²f(0) > 0 at a single point suffices
sol: Leading minors positive for every x gives a positive definite Hessian everywhere
Positive definite Hessian everywhere means strictly convex

parts.ask: Use the first order convexity condition at x = 0 to give a lower bound on f(1, 1).

problems.x: A function with a positive definite Hessian everywhere is strictly convex, and every tangent plane is a global under-estimator.

problems.title: Pareto set and weighted sum
problems.setup: Minimize both f₁ and f₂ over six designs: A(1, 9), B(2, 6), C(4, 5), D(5, 2), E(7, 1), F(5, 6).

parts.ask: Which design is dominated?
w: C, dominated by B at (2, 6)
D, dominated by E at (7, 1)
B, dominated by A at (1, 9)
sol: C(4, 5) is better than F(5, 6) in both objectives
A, B, C, D, E are mutually nondominated: the Pareto set

parts.ask: With weights w = 0.5 on each objective, find the minimum weighted sum value.
sol: Scores 0.5f₁ + 0.5f₂: A 5, B 4, C 4.5, D 3.5, E 4

parts.ask: Which Pareto design does the weighted sum miss for every w ∈ [0, 1]?
w: B, at the knee of the Pareto front
E, at the low f₂ end of the front
A, at the low f₁ end of the front
sol: Segment B to D at f₁ = 4 has f₂ = 3.33, below C's f₂ = 5
C lies above the convex hull, so a linear score always favours B or D

parts.ask: Using the ε-constraint method, minimize f₁ subject to f₂ ≤ 5. Give f₁.

problems.x: Weighted sums find only the convex hull of the Pareto front, while the ε-constraint method reaches nonconvex Pareto points.

problems.title: Nelder Mead iteration
problems.setup: Minimize f = x₁² + x₂² with Nelder Mead from the simplex (1, 1), (0, 2), (3, 2). Use reflection 1, expansion 2 and contraction 0.5.

parts.ask: Find the centroid's x₂ coordinate (centroid of all points except the worst).
Compute f at the reflected point.
Which operation follows, given f_best = 2, f_second worst = 4, f_r = 5, f_worst = 13?
w: Expansion to the point past x_r
Accept x_r directly as new vertex
Shrink all vertices toward the best
sol: f_r ≥ f_second worst rules out acceptance and expansion

parts.ask: Compute f at the outside contraction point.

problems.x: Nelder Mead moves the worst vertex through the centroid using only function values, choosing reflection, expansion or contraction by comparing ranks.

problems.title: Central composite design and main effects
problems.setup: A 2 factor central composite design uses a 2² factorial, axial points and 1 centre point, in coded units. The factorial runs give y(−,−) = 10, y(+,−) = 18, y(−,+) = 14, y(+,+) = 26.

parts.ask: How many runs does the CCD need?
Find the axial distance α for a rotatable design.
Estimate the main effect of factor A from the factorial runs.
Why add axial and centre points to the factorial?
parts.a: To estimate the pure quadratic terms
w: To estimate the AB interaction term
To reduce the total number of runs
To estimate the main effects of A and B
sol: Full quadratic in 2 variables has 6 coefficients
Factorial alone supports linear and interaction terms; axial points give curvature

problems.x: A CCD combines 2^k factorial, 2k axial and centre runs so a full quadratic response surface can be fit, with main effects read from the factorial.

problems.title: Gauss Seidel multidisciplinary analysis
problems.setup: Two coupled disciplines: y₁ = 1 + 0.5y₂ and y₂ = 2 + 0.25y₁. Run block Gauss Seidel (solve y₁ then y₂) starting from y₂ = 0.

parts.ask: Find y₁ after the first iteration's y₁ update.
Find the converged coupled value y₁*.
Find the error reduction factor per iteration.
Which MDO architecture solves this MDA inside every optimizer iteration?
w: IDF (individual discipline feasible)
Collaborative optimization
Analytical target cascading
sol: MDF converges the MDA for each design point
IDF adds coupling targets as design variables with consistency constraints

problems.x: Block Gauss Seidel converges a coupled MDA at a rate set by the product of coupling sensitivities, and MDF wraps that full MDA in the optimizer.
